newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat vows to take measures against corruption.
newsitem.headline: Arafat vows to take measures against corruption.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has vowed to take "all the necessary measures" to curb corruption detailed by lawmakers in a scathing report on his administration.
Arafat made the pledge through an adviser after legislators urged him on Tuesday to sack his entire cabinet and put at least two ministers suspected of wrongdoing on trial.

"The president is studying the recommendations of the committee," Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told reporters. "He will take all the necessary measures to guarantee smooth performance in the Palestinian Authority," he said without elaborating.

The report to the Palestinian Legislative Council, presented by a panel of nine lawmakers, echoed deep disenchantment in the West Bank and Gaza Strip over what is perceived as widespread government corruption, and threatened to cost Arafat crucial international aid.
It recommended trial for Civilian Affairs Minister Jamil al-Tarifi and Planning Minister Nabil Shaath on suspicion of corruption and misuse of power.
The report called for investigations against Transportation Minister Ali Qawasmeh and other senior PLO officials for alleged mismanagement and squandering of public funds.
"The committee recommends to the president of the Palestinian Authority to dissolve the cabinet and form a new cabinet made up of technocrats and qualified people," the report said.
Tarifi said he would submit documents in his defence to the council on Wednesday. Shaath described the allegations as "lies".
"I categorically deny all the accusations and I will prove it with documents. I have nothing to hide," Tarifi told Reuters after the council session.
None of the ministers implicated in the report attended the session.

"Unfortunately, it is all lies and nothing mentioned in the report is true. It is a political demonstration from those who have ambitions to become ministers or want to harm the Palestinian Authority's image internationally," Shaath said.

Countries which have pledged millions of dollars in aid to Arafat's administration since it was established in 1994, including the United States, have set clean governing as a condition for delivering the funds.
The report levelled no allegations of wrongdoing against Arafat.
Its publication coincided with a flurry of diplomatic activity aimed at jump-starting Israel-PLO peace talks, stuck since March over Israeli settlement building in the West Bank.

Israeli political sources said U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross would arrive in the region on Thursday to present Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Washington's ideas for reviving peace efforts.
Western diplomats said Ross would suggest a one-month pause in Israeli settlement activity.
In the West Bank, an Israeli soldier on Tuesday shot dead a Palestinian teenager who stabbed another soldier.
An army spokesman said the Palestinian attacked troops on patrol outside the Elon Moreh settlement near Nablus, drawing gunfire from one of the soldiers.
